book: 114 - American Horror Story and Philosophy - Life Is But a Nightmare

chapters.file: ch09 - The Devil Made Us Write This.md
chapters.relation: The editors' introduction argues that American Horror Story is 'American' in its maximalist excess (the pilot's creepy house, breathing disemboweled cat, and bloody murder), in recycling every major American horror trope from vampires, witches, and ghosts to freak shows and slasher clowns, and in its social commentary on marginalized groups, race relations, and civil rights - so that stripped of horror it is about life in America, and underneath the gore it contains 'a lot of great philosophy', which the book's sixteen chapters extract.

chapters.file: ch10 - I. Goddesses don’t speak in whispers. They scream.md
ch11 - 1. What’s So Scary about Demonic Possession.md
chapters.relation: Using the Asylum possession arc - the boy who rips open the pig's heart, the demon exposing Sister Jude's hit-and-run secret and whispering 'You're Bloody Face' to Thredson, and Sister Mary Eunice's corruption - the chapter argues that possession stories terrify because they break our identity judgments through time, the same judgments on which moral responsibility, criminal punishment (the Manson family parole cases, Phineas Gage), trust, and personal safety depend. Descartes's mind-body union and psychological-continuity theories of identity explain why sameness of body can no longer guarantee sameness of person, and why we fear our own identity being erased next.

Argues that dying in the Murder House or the Hotel Cortez removes death's usual harms - Ben Harmon can reunite with his ghost family and keep counseling patients, and Liz Taylor's chosen death brings reunion with Tristan plus open-ended projects protecting the hotel - but then poses Bernard Williams's boredom problem: finite projects run out over eternity and replacing them would make you a different person. Richard Taylor's Sisyphus and the Hotel's contented Laundress supply the answer that repetitive tasks embraced as meaningful can sustain even an immortal afterlife.

Staged as a remembered backstage conversation among Elsa's freak show performers, the chapter has conjoined twins Bette and Dot work through the Ship of Theseus, the psychological-continuity theory of identity and its coma and false-memory counterexamples, Quine's claim that persons are only convenient posits rather than real entities, split-brain cases suggesting one body can host two minds, and fission worries about what would happen if they were separated - to ask whether they are one person or two, concluding it is a genuine paradox with no agreed answer.

chapters.file: ch14 - 4. How to Live through a Horror Story and Still Find Your Self.md
chapters.relation: A survival guide built on Charles Taylor's philosophy of the self: reality 'discloses' different possibilities depending on one's attunement (Ben Harmon sees the young Moira, the Harmons and the Roanoke families misread their houses), the medieval enchanted cosmos of porous selves explains Sister Mary Eunice's demon, the cursed rubber suit, and Billie Dean Howard's trauma-soaked houses, while the buffered self of the disenchanted universe - Arden locating the devil in the frontal gyrus, John Lowe demanding evidence - invites gaslighting, and full porousness brings its own horrors (Kyle, Cricket). The lesson: keep a pragmatic, open mind and share reality with a community.

Explains Kyle Spencer's horror at the body Madison and Zoe assembled from other people's parts through the history of soul-body theories: Aristotle's De Anima account of the soul as the faculties of a living body (plus the Physiognomonics claim that small people have small minds - poor Ma Petite), Plato's Timaeus on body parts designed for philosophy and reincarnation into bodies fitted to one's vices, Avicenna's soul as a faculty-binding nexus that chooses its bodily vehicle like a vehicle serves its owner, and Merleau-Ponty's habitual body (the Axeman's axe as part of his body, phantom limbs), which best explains why walking around on someone else's legs 'has got to mess with you a little'.

chapters.file: ch16 - II. When bad things keep happening to good people, you start to question what is right and what is wrong.md
ch17 - 6. Horror Can Be Great Drama.md
chapters.relation: Applies Aristotle's Poetics wholesale - mimesis of possible actions, the six elements of tragedy, complete plots of proper magnitude, reversal and recognition, hamartia, and catharsis as the perfecting of fear and pity - to argue that Murder House (Ben's lust as tragic flaw and his double reversal to redemption in death) and Asylum (Sister Jude's irascibility and pride punished then reformed) are genuine high tragedies, and then uses the Nicomachean Ethics (virtue as a mean between extremes; justice as both retributive and rehabilitative) to show the seasons teach virtue, while Coven, Freak Show, and Hotel fall short because their characters' fates are undeserved and the moral message goes murky.

chapters.file: ch18 - 7. And the Most Despicable Jessica Lange Character Is . ..md
chapters.relation: Ranks Jessica Lange's characters from least to most despicable using moral philosophy: Sister Jude earns credit for acting from duty (reporting the Nazi Dr. Arden at personal risk, Kant-style) and for genuinely feeling remorse; Elsa Mars partly honors the matriarchal obligations of care ethics but lacks Aristotle's habitual virtue and moderation, selling Bette and Dot to Dandy for fame; Constance Langdon abuses and effectively murders her disabled children; and Fiona Goode, motivated exclusively by youth, beauty, and power, murders her Supreme and torments Cordelia - never once acting out of concern for others.

chapters.file: ch19 - 8. Night of the Living Disabled.md
chapters.relation: Reads Constance's treatment of Addy and Beau Langdon through the eugenic roots of the horror genre (Angela Smith's Hideous Progeny, The Black Stork, the Production Code): outward bodily difference assumed to prove inner defect, and the disabled treated as better off dead - Addy finding peace only as 'a pretty girl at last' after death, Beau suffocated in the attic. Against the medical model the chapter defends Alison Kafer's political-relational model and crip futurity (Tate's 'He only suffered because of you'), arguing that ableism, not disability itself, makes their lives unlivable and that imagining disabled futures differently is a matter of survival.

Explains Coven's Spirit Wars through the real history and philosophy of New Orleans Voodoo: the historical Marie Laveaux as healer and Voodoo Queen, Tituba as the link between witchcraft and Voodoo in Salem, the loa and spirit possession (Maya Deren's gros bon ange), zombies and the bokor, Papa Legba as trickster gatekeeper rather than Satan, and the seven gates of Guinee. It argues that Laveau's annual innocent and Fiona's failed soul-selling enact the Voodoo cosmology in which hell is the earthly entrapment of the soul - and, as Legba says, 'everybody pays.'

Reads Freak Show through Erving Goffman's Stigma - virtual versus actual social identity, the three types of stigma, discredited versus discreditable conditions, and spoiled identity - and through an analysis of exploitation, dignity, and consent: Elsa's claim that the real monsters are 'the people outside this tent', the courts' defense of freaks' right to perform, and the argument that Ryan Murphy's own casting - real disabled performers as window dressing behind able-bodied stars playing freaks, with roles too scarce for true consent - replicates the exploitation the season condemns, which may be the real horror story.

chapters.file: ch22 - III. I have long stopped asking why the mad do mad things.md

chapters.relation: Voiced by a composite being shredded together from every AHS character, the chapter retells the Buddha's path - Siddhartha sheltered from suffering like a pampered prince, enlightenment as watching 'every episode of American Horror Story', Mara's temptations, and Angulimala with his garland of 999 fingers converted to monkhood - to read Briarcliff's cruelty, Sister Jude's devil, and Bloody Face's son Johnny as suffering born of clinging, in a contingent, moment-to-moment world of karma and rebirth, while Nietzsche's killed God, eternal recurrence, and ressentiment frame the question of who is to blame when there is no creator.

chapters.file: ch24 - 12. A Month from Now, I’ll Be a Balding, Toothless Skeleton.md
chapters.relation: Reads Fiona Goode's war against fading - the experimental RM47 serum, rejecting the Axeman's escape because he would watch her decay, the Papa Legba bargain that collapses because she has no soul - alongside Delphine LaLaurie's blood facials and Marie Laveau's child sacrifices, as illustrations of Buddhist dukkha and the three thirsts (kama for sense pleasure, bhava for existence, vibhava for annihilation). Legba's 'you don't have a soul' becomes an accidentally liberating glimpse of anatta, and Cordelia's dying advice - 'feel the fear... let it all go' - is the mindfulness, echoing Buddhaghosa's corpse meditations, that might have freed Fiona.

Argues Coven is a feminist counterpoint to Aquinas's Natural Law - the reason-grounded doctrine of universal human nature historically wielded against 'unnatural' women, from Zoe's vagina-dentata power to Misty burned in the bayou - and, drawing on Augustine's Confessions ('Things that exist are good', so corruptibility implies goodness to lose) and Lady Macbeth's 'unsex me here', shows that women who are both witch and woman break any single natural moral code; Myrtle Snow, who embraces her double nature and goes 'proudly to the flame', proves Natural Law works only as Cupp-style discernment, not as commandments.

chapters.file: ch26 - IV. I am tough, but I’m no cookie.md
ch27 - 14. The Absurdity at the Heart of Horror.md
chapters.relation: Uses Camus's Myth of Sisyphus to argue that AHS's deepest horror is absurdity - the human quest for meaning in a meaningless universe: the Harmons' doomed attempts to protect each other in the Murder House mirror Sisyphus's futile push, Dr. Arden's experiments on aliens who mock him ('Arden you quack who would make a better duck?') show comprehension of the universe is beyond reach, the Countess's bored immortality and Ma Petite's casual murder stage the confrontation between human longing and a universe that cannot care, and the answer to 'why do bad things happen to good people?' is simply: 'because they do. There is no reason.'

Reads Roanoke through ecocriticism and ecofeminism: the culture-nature dualism collapses as the urban Millers' wooded retreat turns predatory (rain of teeth, pig-men); the Butcher's backstory - a colonial woman starved by men whose blood-sacrifice pact makes the land flourish - aligns women and Nature as co-exploited by patriarchy, with Shelby's 'irrational' warnings ignored and Lee's maternal fury a force of nature; the animalizing of victims (pig-headed roasting, the Polks' barn-raised children, Matt's tryst with the Witch of the Wood) dissolves the human/animal hierarchy; and the media crew's attempt to package wilderness for ratings ends with Nature striking back at Agnes in the woods.

chapters.file: ch29 - 16. Please Don’t Kill Me! (But if You Do, Could You Make a Video ).md
chapters.relation: Reads Roanoke through Stephen Cave's Mortality Paradox, Ernest Becker's Denial of Death, and Terror Management Theory: the Blood Moon ghosts embody inevitable death, dramatic irony mirrors our denial, reality-TV fame and Twitter followers are the modern immortality project (Agnes's 'I just wanted to be on TV', the superfans killed mid-broadcast), and the Polks' ritual cannibalism is symbolic power over extinction. Montaigne's 'to study philosophy is to learn to die' and his savoring of fleeting moments close the chapter, with Shelby - who alone submits to death without fiction - as the figure who actually escapes the terror.

A companion travelogue cataloging real haunted American sites paralleling each season - the Los Feliz Murder House and Winchester Mystery House behind Murder House, the Trans-Allegheny Asylum and Waverly Hills Sanatorium behind Asylum, Marie Laveau's tomb in St. Louis Cemetery #1 behind Coven, the Stanley Hotel of The Shining - from haunted houses, asylums, cemeteries, and prisons to the RMS Queen Mary and the Lizzie Borden B&B. It argues hauntings are a pervasive feature of American history and folklore, and makes no philosophical argument of its own.

holes.name: Richard Taylor
holes.what: Twentieth-century American philosopher whose Good and Evil argues that a life of repetitive toil, like Sisyphus's, is meaningful provided the agent embraces the task as its own end.
holes.why: Chapter 2's answer to the boredom of ghostly immortality in the Hotel Cortez rests on Taylor's Sisyphus argument alongside Bernard Williams's, and he is cited by name.

holes.name: Charles Taylor
holes.what: Canadian philosopher whose Sources of the Self and A Secular Age describe the shift from porous selves in an enchanted, hierarchical cosmos to buffered selves in a disenchanted, mechanistic universe.
holes.why: Chapter 4 is built entirely on Taylor's framework - self-interpreting animals, attunement, enchanted and disenchanted worlds - to explain who survives an American Horror Story.

holes.name: Porous and Buffered Selves
holes.what: Taylor's distinction between a self open to outside forces and independently meaningful reality (porous) and a self walled off inside a mind-imposed, disenchanted world (buffered).
holes.why: Chapter 4 uses the porous/buffered contrast to explain why believers in the supernatural survive haunted houses while disenchanted skeptics get gaslit, and why becoming porous again is costly.

holes.name: Physiognomy
holes.what: The doctrine, reaching back to Greek medicine and the pseudo-Aristotelian Physiognomonics, that outward bodily features reveal moral character and inner faculties.
holes.why: Chapter 5 frames the whole body-soul question with physiognomy, using it to explain why Kyle rejects his reassembled body and to mock Aristotle's claim that small people have small minds.

holes.name: Aristotle's Poetics (tragedy theory)
holes.what: Aristotle's theory of tragedy in the Poetics: mimesis of possible actions, the six formal elements, complete plots with reversal and recognition, hamartia, and the catharsis of fear and pity.
holes.why: Chapter 6's entire defense of Murder House and Asylum as great drama is a chapter-length application of the Poetics, which the taxonomy lacks.

holes.name: Alison Kafer
holes.what: Feminist disability scholar whose Feminist, Queer, Crip develops the political-relational model of disability and the politics of crip futurity against ableist assumptions about the future.
holes.why: Chapter 8 reads Addy's and Beau Langdon's fates almost entirely through Kafer's critique of cure-only futures and her insistence that ableism, not disability, is the harm.

holes.name: Eugenics
holes.what: The movement to improve the human gene pool by controlling reproduction, historically entwined with institutionalization, sterilization, and letting disabled infants die.
holes.why: Chapter 8 argues the modern horror genre was born from eugenic assumptions (The Black Stork, the Production Code) that Constance's treatment of her children reenacts.

holes.name: Voodoo (Vodun / Vodou / New Orleans Voodoo)
holes.what: African-diaspora religious philosophy of Benin, Haiti, and Louisiana centered on serving the loa, spirit possession, ancestral connection, healing, and the crossing between the living and the dead.
holes.why: Chapter 9 explains Coven's Spirit Wars through Voodoo metaphysics - loa, possession, Papa Legba, zombies, and the gates of Guinee - none of which the taxonomy covers.

holes.name: Erving Goffman
holes.what: Sociologist whose Stigma (1963) analyzes socially discrediting attributes, virtual versus actual social identity, and the management of spoiled identity.
holes.why: Chapter 10's entire reading of Freak Show - stigmatized performers, exploitation, and the show's own casting - is an application of Goffman's stigma theory.

holes.name: Stigma (spoiled identity)
holes.what: An attribute that reduces its bearer in others' eyes from a whole and usual person to a tainted, discounted one, spoiling social identity and limiting life chances.
holes.why: Chapter 10 uses stigma's types (abominations of the body, blemishes of character, tribal stigma) to explain both the fictional freak show and the real one AHS mounts on television.

holes.name: Ernest Becker
holes.what: Cultural anthropologist whose The Denial of Death argues that human culture is an elaborate 'hero system' of symbolic immortality projects built to deny the terror of mortality.
holes.why: Chapter 16 reads Roanoke's cannibals, cultists, and reality-TV stars as Becker-style death deniers, and Becker anchors the chapter alongside Terror Management Theory.

holes.name: Terror Management Theory (TMT)
holes.what: The experimental program (Greenberg, Pyszczynski, Solomon) built on Becker: mortality salience drives worldview defense, self-esteem striving, violence, and symbolic immortality projects.
holes.why: Chapter 16 cites TMT studies to explain Roanoke's murders, cults, and craving for screen time as defenses against the fear of death.
